title: Heavier Every Monday
blurb: Dagny gives up two zones to hold one, and the sum she does out loud shows her who has been throwing Drops, but the Weighman has been doing sums of his own.

blocks.text: Three Pins on the Ninepins' wall, one Anchor to hold them, and the one Anchor was me.
I stood at the Lip rail ten minutes before the bell with the team round me, and I said it out loud, because they had to hear exactly what I was giving up.
"L6," I said. "I hold L6 the whole Drop. L2 and L4 stay true down. Nobody's hand goes near them."
Nobody spoke. My throat was tight, and my left hand was shut in the pocket of my father's lift-coat round nothing at all.

"Everything that reaches a well comes through L6 last," I said. "It's the bottom zone. Under it there's only the Throat. So I hold the bottom, and I give up everything above the L5 ledge. Up there, whatever Hobbs Rise set, nobody sets against them. Dunnet, you're alone up there. Pru, anything Hobbs Rise do up top, Hobbs Rise pay for, every pound of it, and I don't. Price it that way."
"Shovellers evens," Pru said. "Us six-to-four against. Price stands."

Half an hour before, the Weighman had stood me on the Lip scale and written about a stone of carry against my name in the league book. My bones held about three. Three is the sore line. It sits in the ankles first and then behind the knees, and it was there before I had touched a Pin, put there by a week of lean-weight coming in an ounce an hour while I slept and ate and walked to the shaft, and no scale in Scarrow could tell it from carry.
Hal sat on an upturned crate by the rail with his ribs strapped under his shirt. He was stood down until the bone mended, and he watched me the way he watches a rope he doesn't trust.
"Steady," he said. It was the kindest I had ever heard him say it.
Rafe stood beside him with his hands in his pockets. The debt had gone to ninety-two crowns that morning. He knew it and I knew it, and neither of us said it.
"They've only the one Cob," he said. "One Anchor's plenty, isn't it, Dags?"
I loved him for trying. It didn't reach my hands.

Pru tapped her scouting chalk on the rail and nodded down the Lip at the Shovellers. "Their Dropper's Absalom Hurd," she said. "Registered at sixteen stone. They've played him the same way three weeks running. He takes the Cob, he comes down the wall over your well, and he dares your Anchor to turn him."
"Hobbs Rise lowered him in on the coal skip, I heard," Dunnet said. "Took the whole village on the winch."
It was a joke about the other side and it was for us, and Lisbet snorted. I looked at Absalom Hurd. He was the widest man I had ever seen on a Lip, and he was grinning.

A head and a half. With the Cob in his arms, two heads. Two stone a minute to whoever turned him. I had three stone between me and Heavy for the whole match, and no second Anchor to share a pound of it.
Osk's chair stood by the ladder with its ring of grit round the legs. He waited until I looked at him.
"One," he said. "Hold the bottom. Two. Pay for nothing they'll pay for. Three." He stopped, the way he does before the word he means. "Come back up."

Lisbet lowered me to L6 in the sling. I put my right hand on the Pin and held true down. True down costs nothing, whoever is in it. But a held true down still counts in a Lap, and I knew it, and I kept the sum ready.
On the far wall above me, their Anchor, Nell Varrow, held L5. Their other Anchor, a boy with a shaved head, held L3.
The bell.

The Cob came down the centre out of the dark. Absalom Hurd dived and took it in the top zones like a man catching a sack off a cart, and the boy on L3 set across at our wall and carried him over. I counted it while it happened. Two heads, turned by their Anchor, on their bill. Absalom hit our rope by L4 and came down it hand under hand with the Cob crooked in one arm, and when he reached L5's zone, Varrow set straight at our wall and pressed him flat to it so he could climb easy.
So she was paying for him too.

Dunnet came down our rope underneath Absalom, into the Lap above my ledge, and stopped there, between Absalom and my zone. Fifteen stone of him on one rope. There's no passing fifteen stone on one rope.

Now the sum. In that Lap, my true down and Varrow's across added together, a plumb and a half on the slant, and while my hand was on the Pin, half of whatever hung there was mine. I wasn't going to turn Absalom Hurd. Not one count.
I did the Release, the way Osk taught me, breath and hand together, little finger last, and I took my hand off the Pin.

True down never adds. With my hand off, Varrow's set ruled the whole Lap by itself, one plumb across, and every pound in it was hers. Absalom came down onto Dunnet's shoulders and stopped. Absalom, the Cob and Dunnet: three and a half heads, three and a half stone a minute, all of it on Varrow.

It was a gamble, and I knew the size of it. My zone was true down now. If Absalom got past Dunnet with the Cob, he only had to let go and fall straight into our well. Three points to them. I watched the loose tail of our rope where it lay pressed against the wall in the lamplight, because a rope tells you what a field is doing, and I counted. Ten counts. Twenty. Thirty.
At forty-one the rope's tail swung off the wall and hung straight.
Varrow had let go. Nobody holds three and a half stone a minute for long.

Absalom let go of the rope to drop past Dunnet, and as he went by, Dunnet hooked the Cob out from under his arm, clean, the way you take a loaf off a shelf. Absalom fell on without it, straight down into the Throat beside our well, and he had nothing in his arms when he landed.

I gripped. One count before it would turn. Three counts for the quarter-turn across. Dunnet hung on our rope with the Cob for those four counts and didn't move, and they were the longest four counts I have ever stood through.
"Across, Dunnet," Pru shouted. "Evens, all yours."

He let go. My set carried him and the Cob over the shaft to the Shovellers' wall, two heads on my bill, a stone every half-minute, and I felt each pound arrive in my ankles. He took their rope and went down it into the Throat, and the Cob went into their well. Twenty counts.
Three to nil. I did the Release.
Absalom Hurd had held the Cob for a minute and a half, and in all that time I had not paid one pound to move him.
At the Hoist the Weighman read the book aloud as he wrote. "Varrow. Three stone one." Then me. "Quillon. One stone twelve."
My bones said three stone ten, near enough, and my ankles agreed with them. But Absalom Hurd had cost Hobbs Rise more than he had cost me, and that was what I had said on the Lip, and it was true.
"Counts," Dunnet said, grinning, "you made their Anchor pay for the big lad's supper."

Walls swapped for Drop 2. We had the odd wall now. I took L5, the lowest Pin we had, and left L1 and L3 true. Varrow went down to L6, below me on the far wall, and set it straight at our wall. The boy took L4.

Hobbs Rise had learned. Absalom came down our rope before the Cob did and stopped in my zone, three metres above my ledge, with nothing in his arms. He was there to cost me. Anything I set while he hung there, I paid a head and a half for.
The Cob came down and Dunnet took it high and came down our rope with it, sure-handed, the same hands that had hooked it off Absalom.
"Big lad below you, Dunnet," Pru called. "Long odds on staying. Over, now."

I turned L5 straight across at the Shovellers' wall. Three counts for the quarter-turn, and every one of them on my bill: Dunnet and the Cob, two heads. Absalom hanging in my zone, a head and a half. Three and a half stone a minute. When the set came square, Dunnet let go of our rope with the Cob in both arms, and my set took him out across the shaft. I counted. Four.
Two metres out from our wall, the Cob left Dunnet.
It didn't drop. It went back. It went two metres back the way he had come, against my set, to our wall, into Absalom Hurd's arms.
I said it out loud on the ledge before I knew I was going to.
"That's not a slip."

Then the sum, aloud, because saying it was the only way I could make myself believe it. "Nothing in L5 points at our wall. I set it at theirs. You let go of a thing while you're falling and it falls with you. It stays at your elbow. It doesn't leave. That went two metres back against a full plumb to the one man waiting for it. Nothing in my zone carries a Cob to our wall. You did, Dunnet."
It hurt to say. It hurt in my chest, as if a hand were pressing there and wouldn't lift.
Dunnet hit the far wall and caught their rope and hung there, and didn't look at me.

Absalom had the Cob on our rope, in my zone, and my set was dragging him off the wall, and he held on. I couldn't keep him off our well. Below my ledge the zone was Varrow's, set at our wall. All my set could do was make him climb down against it while I paid three and a half stone a minute for every count he and Dunnet spent in my zone, and I had barely two stone left between me and Heavy. I couldn't buy that Drop. It had already been sold.
My father used to call out a load that was wrong in the cage before he let the cage move. I said it under my breath, to him.
"Bad load in the cage, Da. Hold the brake."
I did the Release and let go. Absalom climbed down our wall in true down, Varrow's set took him the rest of the way, and the Cob went into our well.
Three all.
Lisbet hauled me up in the sling. Her mouth was tight. She said, "Move," to nobody, and I didn't know if she had heard me on the ledge or seen it for herself.

Dunnet came up the rope last. He didn't go to the rail. The Weighman had his back to us at the scale, weighing the Shovellers, and Dunnet came to Osk's chair, where I stood with one hand on its arm because my ankles wanted somewhere to put me, and he stopped in front of me. His face was white.
"Dagny Quillon," he said.
He has never called me that. He calls me Counts.

"You did the sum right," he said. "I let it go to him. On purpose." He looked at the planks. "Sibbald Teague holds my mother's book. The house on Gantry Lane, the rent, all of it. Every Drop I throw for him, he marks the book down."
My hands went hot and then they shook. The anger came up into my throat so fast I had to swallow before I could speak.
"How many?" I said.
"Two. The first Drop against the Tanners. And this one."
I thought of him a body-length slow off his rope in the Tanners' first Drop, and laughing about it. I thought of him behind the Lip shed with the boy in the grey scarf.
"The note behind the shed," I said. "I saw you."
He shut his eyes. "The note says which Drop. The coin's his mark, so I know the note's from him."

"Rafe owed that man ninety-two crowns this morning," I said, and my voice was too loud and I couldn't make it quieter. "Every Drop you sell him is a match we could lose, and a lost match pays none of us anything. You sold him my brother's week."
Rafe had come up beside me. He had gone very still.
"He's got you on a book too, then?" he said.
"Rafe Quillon," Dunnet said. "I'm sorry."

Then I looked at him properly, and the anger didn't go, but something else came in beside it and sat down with it. He is twenty-two. He has five brothers and sisters and a mother in a row-house on Gantry Lane, and Teague's book over all of them, and he had stood on a Lip every Monday this spring knowing what the note in his pocket said. That is a weight. I know what weight does to a body. It made my eyes sting, and I let them.
Osk's chair creaked. Everyone went quiet, because he had lowered his voice.
"One," Osk said. "He plays the third Drop. Two." He waited. "Straight. Three. We talk on Tuesday. All of us."
Pru was looking at her chalk. She said nothing at all.
"Can you?" I asked Dunnet. "Straight?"
"Aye," he said. "He'll know by tonight."
"Then he'll know," I said.

Three all meant a coin for the walls. Pru called it and won it, and I took the even wall and L6 again, and Varrow took L5 again, with more than three stone in her book now and less appetite for big men.

Hobbs Rise didn't send Absalom down our wall a second time. Dunnet took the Cob at the top, and their boy on L3 set across and carried him over to our wall, paying for it, and Dunnet held the Cob in both arms and came down our rope with it like a man carrying a child. He came down through the Lap hand over hand against Varrow's set and into my zone, and he said, "Counts," once, quietly. I set across. He let go.
Fifteen counts on my bill, two heads, and he went down the Shovellers' wall and into their well at four minutes and ten.
Six to three.
I did the Release, and my ankles gave out, and I sat down on L6 with my back to the wall and counted what I had left. Four stone twelve, by my count. Heavy was a stone and two pounds away.

On the Lip the Weighman paid us five crowns each. I put mine straight into Rafe's hand. "Against the ninety-two," I said. He closed his fingers on it and didn't make a joke, and I loved him for that too.
Dunnet held his five crowns in his open hand and looked at them as if they weighed more than they did.
Pru came and stood by me at the rail while Lisbet coiled the sling. Off the shaft she talks flat and plain, as if the patter costs her something.

"Coldhithe's our last match," she said. "Away. Their shaft's built wrong. L3 and L4 sit on the same wall, one over the other. They call it the Twin Ledge. Whoever has that wall has a Lap made of two of their own Pins, and nobody else gets a say in it."
Two Pins on one wall, one Lap. I counted our Anchors, and got one, and Hal on a crate.
"Last thing, Miss Quillon," the Weighman called. "Scale."
I stood on it. He wrote the number, and then he didn't close the book. He ran his finger up the column of my Monday weights, slowly, one Monday at a time, and he frowned.
"You've not Settled, Miss Quillon," he said. "Four weeks, and you're heavier every Monday. The Settle's free."
